idiom_name: @variable on the class object + class << self accessors
implementation_notes: Ruby stores the shared state as an instance variable of the class object itself: @level defined in the class body and read through accessors defined on the singleton class (class << self; attr_accessor :level; end), with instance methods delegating to self.class.level. The ruby-lang FAQ recommends class instance variables over class variables because @@variables are shared between a class and all its subclasses, so a subclass reassignment silently changes the parent. What replaces the classic structure is this per-class storage plus the delegation methods; each class in a hierarchy gets its own slot, and the state is per process.
code_sketch:
class LogSettings
  @level = 1                                 # state on the class object
  class << self; attr_accessor :level; end   # singleton-class accessors

  def level; self.class.level; end           # delegates upward
  def set_level(value); self.class.level = value; end
end

a = LogSettings.new; b = LogSettings.new
a.set_level(3)
b.level          # => 3
pitfalls: Inherited methods run with self.class set to the subclass, whose @level is nil unless it is initialized - the classic Ruby inheritance surprise; initialize the state in each class or read it from the defining class.
The singleton-class accessors are public, so any code can reassign the shared state; make them private if only the class should write.
The state is per process: forked children and isolated runtimes get their own copy, so this is not shared memory.

variants.name: Class variable @@state shared through the whole hierarchy
variants.implementation_notes: The literal translation of making all data members static in Ruby is a class variable: @@level is accessible from both instance and class methods and is shared by the class, its subclasses and their instances. What it buys is direct access without the self.class hop; what it costs is the FAQ's warning - @@state is one slot for the entire hierarchy, so a subclass that reassigns it changes the base class's state too. Choose it only when the hierarchy is deliberately one monostate (a process-wide counter), never as the default.
variants.code_sketch:
class LogSettings
  @@level = 1

  def level; @@level; end                 # visible from instances
  def set_level(value); @@level = value; end
end

a = LogSettings.new; b = LogSettings.new
a.set_level(3)
b.level          # => 3
pitfalls: A class variable is one slot for the whole hierarchy: a subclass that assigns it changes the base class's state as well (the documented Woof/LoudWoof surprise).
@@ is readable from both instances and class methods, so encapsulation is convention only, and a reopened class or module can re-declare the same variable accidentally.
Class variables are not visible across processes and are a classic source of accidental global state; prefer the class-instance-variable variant unless the hierarchy really is one monostate.
